Gloria Steinem, who has died aged 92, was a writer, community organiser, political campaigner and a charismatic feminist activist who called herself “an entrepreneur of social change”. She spent much of her life on the road, often accompanied by equally committed fellow campaigners. Steinem loathed public speaking, but during two years travelling in India in her 20s, she moved from village to village, with “a sari, a cup and a comb” in a group countering religious intolerance. She said she learned then, as Gandhi taught, that a message was all the more powerful delivered “eye to eye”.

Steinem, unlike some of her contemporaries, never recanted or modified her many causes, which included civil rights, violence against women, and the struggle for equality. She continued to argue that every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction, and an understanding of the patriarchal instinct to restrict a woman’s right to contraception and abortion.

articles.title: Qué hacer si se impugna tu voto: consejos prácticos para las elecciones de mitad de legislatura
articles.author:
<name>Karen Figueroa-Clewett, Lecturer, Agents of Change program, Department of Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/karen-figueroa-clewett-1389481"/>
paras: Ahora que las elecciones de mitad de legislatura de 2026 entran en su recta final, es importante que conozcas tus derechos por si se impugna tu voto.

La mejor manera de asegurarte de que tu voto se tenga en cuenta es defender tus propios intereses. Soy abogada y profesor de la iniciativa de defensa de los derechos civiles para estudiantes universitarios de la Universidad del Sur de California , Agents of Change. A continuación te indico varias formas sencillas de asegurarte de que tu voto se cuente y dos soluciones prácticas que puedes considerar si tu voto sigue siendo objeto de impugnación.

Una parte fundamental para asegurarte de que puedas votar consiste en realizar los preparativos necesarios antes incluso de llegar al colegio electoral. Sigue leyendo para saber cómo y dónde inscribirte, dónde y cuándo puedes votar, y a qué números llamar si necesitas información que no encuentres en Internet.

Antes de votar, debe asegurarse de que está registrado para votar. Puede verificar el estatus de su registro utilizando esta herramienta en línea . Si no puede usar una herramienta en línea, llame a su oficina electoral local o a una línea de ayuda para votantes como las que se enumeran en una sección a continuación.

Si se da cuenta de que no está registrado, puede usar esta herramienta de la Conferencia Nacional de Legislaturas Estatales para encontrar la solicitud de registro en línea de su estado. Si necesita hacer esto en persona, llame a su oficina electoral local para recibir instrucciones.
Para este momento, es posible que ya haya pasado la fecha límite para el registro de votantes en su estado. Pero puede que no sea demasiado tarde para que se registre.

Muchos estados permiten el registro el mismo día en el sitio de votación. Puede encontrar las leyes de su estado sobre el día de la votación detalladas aquí . Pídale al trabajador electoral, en el centro de votación que le corresponda, un formulario de registro para el mismo día; complete el formulario y luego solicite una “boleta condicional”. Una boleta condicional permite a los funcionarios electorales contabilizar su voto después de verificar su elegibilidad como votante. Si no puede buscar en línea, puede llamar a su oficina electoral local para averiguar si puede registrarse el mismo día de las elecciones.
Las leyes de identificación de votantes generalmente se refieren a la votación en persona, no las boletas en ausencia ni las boletas enviadas por correo.

Si vive en un estado que requiere verificar la identidad para el voto en persona, reúna los documentos requeridos, que pueden variar desde licencias de conducir hasta estados de cuenta bancarios con información de identificación, antes de dirigirse al lugar de votación que le corresponda. Puede encontrar la información de contacto de la oficina electoral de su condado aquí . Esta página web incluye una tabla que enumera los documentos de identificación aceptables de cada estado y las posibles excepciones para algunas personas. También puede llamar a su oficina electoral local para averiguar qué se requiere.
Votantes ausentes: Localice las normas de verificación de identidad de su estado aquí .

Puede asegurarse de que se dirige al lugar de votación correcto con esta herramienta . O llame a la oficina electoral de su condado para encontrar el centro de votación que le corresponde y su horario de operación; puede buscar la información de contacto de la oficina electoral de su condado aquí .

Una vez que sepa cuál es su lugar de votación y su horario, puede ir allí y registrarse. En la mayoría de los casos, se le entregará una boleta, se le mostrará dónde votar y se le pedirá que deposite su boleta en una máquina o una urna, luego de lo cual podrá continuar alegremente con su vida.
Es en el momento del registro donde las cosas pueden salir mal.
Aquí se presentan posibles problemas al momento de votar y formas de solucionarlos.
Posibilidad #1: Máquinas de votación descompuestas.
Si le piden que se vaya debido a que las máquinas se descompusieron, no se vaya. Pida que le den una boleta de papel.
Posibilidad #2: Está esperando en la fila y los funcionarios informan que el centro de votación ha cerrado.

Si llego a la fila del centro de votación antes de que cerrara, no permita que lo rechacen a la hora del cierre si no ha votado. Tiene el derecho legal de votar en esas circunstancias, así que permanezca en la fila y espere para emitir su voto .
Posibilidad #3: No está en la lista de votantes registrados.

Si le dicen que no puede votar porque su nombre no está en la lista de votantes, pídale al trabajador del sitio de votación que verifique nuevamente y que revise la lista de votantes suplementarios. Si aún no logran encontrar su nombre, pídale al trabajador electoral que verifique si usted se encuentra en el lugar correcto.
Posibilidad #4: Alguien dice que no tiene derecho a votar.

Si su elegibilidad para votar sigue siendo cuestionada pese a que está seguro de estar en el lugar de votación correcto, solicite emitir un voto provisional , que está disponible en todos los estados, excepto en Idaho y Minnesota. Puede encontrar detalles sobre las reglas de votación provisional de su estado aquí .
Haga un seguimiento de su boleta provisional aquí .

Si no recibe una boleta provisional, llame a una línea de ayuda para obtener asistencia electoral. Aquí hay cuatro líneas directas, administradas por miembros de la coalición no partidista Protección Electoral , que pueden ayudarlo:
Inglés: 866-OUR-VOTE/866-687-8683, The Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law
Español: 888-VE-Y-VOTA/888-839-8682, Fondo de Educación de la Asociación Nacional de Funcionarios Latinos Electos y Designados
Idiomas asiáticos: 888-API-VOTE/888-274-8683, Voto Estadounidense de Asiáticos e Isleños del Pacífico
Árabe: 844-YALLA-US/844-925-5287, Instituto Árabe Estadounidense

Si alguien trata de asustarlo para que vote o para que no vote por un candidato, manténgase firme y exija una boleta en el sitio de votación, llame a una línea de ayuda para denunciar la intimidación y más tarde presente una queja por teléfono ante el FBI al 800-CALL-FBI - 800-225-5324 - o por internet en tips.fbi.gov .

Si aún no se le permite votar, considere emprender acciones legales, aunque primero obtenga asesoramiento sobre su situación particular en una de las líneas de ayuda, que cuentan con abogados gratuitos. Es buena idea anotar los nombres de las personas que le impidieron votar y pedir a las personas que presenciaron el incidente su información de contacto.

articles.title: Do you need to worry about the Sun turning into a black hole?
articles.author:
<name>Anuradha Gupta, Assistant Professor of Physics & Astronomy, University of Mississippi</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/anuradha-gupta-2744412"/>
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
Do I need to worry about the sun turning into a black hole? – Anonymous٫ age 7٫ Chicago٫ Illinois
At the end of their lifespans, some massive stars collapse under their own weight until they turn into a black hole that sucks up everything around it.

It’s a dramatic conclusion to a star’s billions of years of existence, but it’s not the finale that our own Sun will have. Our solar system’s star is not big enough to have that kind of outcome, so worrying about the Sun becoming a black hole doesn’t need to be on your list of anxieties. Whatever happens to the Sun will happen very slowly, over billions of years. By that time, you’ll be long gone. Humans might not be there to witness it at all.
As an astrophysicist, I am fascinated by black holes and how they form. The universe is filled with different kinds of stars, and each has a distinct tale to tell about its life.
Just like humans, stars have a life cycle. A star is born when a giant gas cloud collapses in on itself and then grows, shining light by burning fuel.

In its core, the baby star fuses four atoms of hydrogen together to form the element helium, which releases energy in the form of starlight. This fuel-burning process also exerts outward pressure against gravity, which is pulling in on the star. These competing forces give stars their round shape.

As the star grows older, it eventually burns up all the hydrogen inside it. At this point, it can’t maintain the same outward push, so gravity squeezes the star, shrinking it smaller and smaller. The helium atoms inside are pushed closer together, and they start to fuse into heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen, iron and more.

The star keeps burning its fuel and shining on until most of the helium in its core has fused into iron. But fusing together multiple atoms of iron requires taking in energy instead of releasing it, so at this point, the fuel burning stops.

Gravity then takes over, and the core of the star collapses rapidly in a dramatic explosion. The cores of heavier stars are extremely dense, so any material falling toward the collapsing star bounces off, producing shock waves. This phenomenon drives what is called a core-collapse supernova explosion . The star explodes, shooting elements like oxygen and other heavy elements off into space . What remains is a dead star with a small, dense core.

The type of dead star the collapse forms depends on how much mass the star started with. If the mass is less than roughly eight times the mass of the Sun, the collapse will leave behind a white dwarf . This is a star so dense that all the electrons inside it are squeezed extremely close together, until they are no longer bound to individual atoms.

If the star was about eight to 20 times the mass of the Sun, it would leave behind a neutron star , which is an even denser star. In a neutron star, the electrons and protons crush together to produce neutrons.
If the star is heavier than 20 times the mass of the Sun, the end product will be a black hole with gravitational pull so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape past its boundary.

Because our Sun is on the smaller side for a star, when it dies it will collapse into a white dwarf, roughly the same size as Earth. It will still shine some light at first, but over time it may slowly cool down, to eventually become a cold, dark object called a black dwarf .

In about 1 billion years from now, the Sun will start to grow hotter and brighter than it is today. As it shines more brightly, the sunlight it casts on Earth will increase, which will make the Earth hotter. The oceans will evaporate, and it will become very difficult to sustain life as we know it on Earth.

In about 5 billion years, all the hydrogen in the Sun’s core will run out. The core will then contract under gravity, while the hydrogen continues to fuse in a shell around it. This will cause the outer layer of the Sun to expand enormously and enter a phase known as the red giant . During this phase, the Sun will grow so big that it could potentially run into Earth’s orbit.

Scientists don’t yet know if Earth will be swallowed by the Sun at this point. But even if Earth evades being gulped up, the Sun’s heat will toast everything on Earth, and no complex life will be able to survive.
This may sound scary, but you don’t have to worry, because humans will probably be long gone by the time the Sun starts consuming Earth’s atmosphere .

Earth was formed about 4.6 billion years ago , and if you imagine its entire lifespan up to now as a single day, then all of human history happened in the last six seconds. There’s still about 26 hours to go before the Sun becomes a red giant.

Suppose the Sun were to become a black hole today, all of sudden. Assuming the black hole had the same mass as the Sun, humans would not be in immediate danger. Earth and all other planets would feel the same gravitational pull as from the Sun.
Only objects very close to the black hole – within a few miles or so – would be sucked in. Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, has an orbit of about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers).
This means there is no immediate danger from the Sun turning into a black hole, even hypothetically.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: Stars and Stripes shows how government-funded journalism can work – if it’s free to report the truth
articles.author:
<name>Cindy Elmore, Professor of Journalism, East Carolina University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/cindy-elmore-2760615"/>
paras: As local and national news outlets continue to disappear across the U.S. , I’d always thought that the military newspaper Stars and Stripes offered one model for a partial solution: government financial support.
But this approach only works if those who believe in the free press – including elected officials – offer unconditional support.

On Aug. 21, 2026, the Pentagon fired the publisher, editor and a reporter at Stars and Stripes, citing insubordination and unauthorized media appearances. But the firings took place after the outlet ran a string of articles that cast the Pentagon in a poor light.
The newspaper, which is often simply called Stripes, has served overseas military forces and their families since 1918 , with a 23-year break between World War I and World War II.

It has continuously remained in print since World War II, providing Americans serving overseas on American military bases everywhere from Okinawa to the Azores with news on topics ranging from high school football games to troop deployments.

When I was a reporter at Stars and Stripes in the late 1990s, I covered both the good and the bad from Bosnia and Kosovo during the NATO peacekeeping missions: the armed unit that doled out cash to Bosnians after the military ran over their farm animals; the soldiers who guarded a school so that the children of separate ethnic groups could attend together; and the military contractors who received no-bid contracts.

While some big stories are also written about in other news outlets covering the military, many of them are only discovered because Stars and Stripes’ civilian and military journalists work and live alongside service members in Europe, the Middle East and the Pacific.
It’s the very same premise behind good local newspapers: There’s little meaningful journalism about local issues without journalists who live and work in the communities they cover.

Stripes was able to provide the only eyewitness account of the negotiations that led to Germany’s surrender in 1945 because its reporter was in the schoolhouse in Reims, France, where Allied and German officials hashed out the terms.

Stripes journalists were also on the front lines of the Vietnam War, with The New York Times describing Stars and Stripes as the only military information outlet giving American troops in Vietnam a candid account of the war’s progress .

More recently, a Stripes reporter based in Bahrain was able to report how U.S. military families were experiencing Iranian drone attacks in Manama , which hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. She was able to report on the attacks firsthand because she was right there , evacuating alongside them.
It was another Stars and Stripes journalist who first reported on the problems aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln in July and August 2026.

The aircraft carrier was in the midst of an exceedingly long deployment due to the U.S.-Iran war. There had been food and water shortages, disrupted mail service and long, grueling workdays with little time off. Some sailors were experiencing mental health struggles , and at least one jumped overboard.

The reporter, Alison Bath, who is based at the headquarters of the U.S. Navy’s Sixth Fleet in Naples, Italy, had interviewed active-duty sailors and family members of sailors aboard the ship. She explained how she had reviewed “ dozens of public social media comments and posts by crew members.”
Bath’s story and the follow-up accounts from other media outlets clearly angered Hegseth, who said it “ completely misrepresented ” the situation.

The media frenzy over the USS Lincoln largely overshadowed the work of another Stripes journalist, Lara Korte, who reported on the hardships, confusion and financial costs endured by military families who had to suddenly evacuate from U.S. Central Command headquarters in Bahrain starting on March 2, 2026.

Like Bath, Korte had interviewed several military family members, one of whom shared with Korte the audio recording of a virtual town hall meeting that the military held for the families. A Navy admiral said on the recording that the military “was in uncharted territory” and had little guidance for families who didn’t know where to live or how to retrieve their cars and belongings.
Though the Pentagon didn’t dispute Korte’s reporting, she was fired for “insubordination” alongside the editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and publisher, Max Lederer, on Aug. 21.

Unlike most shuttered or shrunken news outlets whose advertising model was upended by the internet , Stars and Stripes has long been shielded from market forces thanks to a subsidy from the Department of Defense that covers roughly half its budget .
While this funding could be seen as anathema to journalistic independence, the U.S. government has mandated since the 1950s that the paper have editorial freedom.

Even before then, U.S. military leaders protected the newspaper’s independence. Gen. John J. Pershing , who commanded the American Expeditionary Forces in Europe during World War I, and Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, who commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II, each ordered military commanders not to interfere with the newspaper . So did Navy Adm. John S. McCain Jr. , father of the late Sen. John McCain and the commander‐in‐chief of U.S. Pacific Command during the Vietnam War.
That’s not what’s happening under the Trump administration.

In March 2026 , the Pentagon instituted new guidelines requiring that Stripes content be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.” The following month, the department fired Jacqueline Smith , the newspaper’s ombudsman charged with protecting its editorial independence.
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell described the moves as part of an effort to “refocus” the outlet away from “ woke distractions that siphon morale .”

There’s always been a struggle between military leaders who want to control the reporting at Stripes and those who recognize that freedom of the press is exactly the kind of right that the U.S. military fights for.
Many current and former military commanders see a real benefit in the outlet’s editorial independence because of the values it communicates and the information it provides

Retired Army Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling is one such supporter. In an Aug. 25, 2026, article in The Bulwark website, he described the ways in which he relied on the newspaper’s reporting when he was a commander in Europe.

“Every major military command has an extensive communications apparatus,” Hertling wrote, “but none of those organizations can manufacture credibility. Credibility comes from readers believing that when something goes wrong, somebody will tell them. That’s why Stripes’ early reporting on the USS Abraham Lincoln was so important.”

On Aug. 27, the fired publisher, editor and reporter filed a lawsuit against Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, the Defense Department, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and another public affairs official, Andrew Brey, alleging that they were fired in retaliation for news coverage that was unflattering to the military. The suit argues that this violated both their protected rights to free speech and Department of Defense policies and regulations.
The department hasn’t specifically responded to the allegations, but it did agree to a one-week reprieve of paid administrative leave as a federal judge considers the lawsuit.

The three journalists are being represented by the same legal team that represents the fired former employees of Voice of America, another government-funded news source that the Trump administration attempted to dismantle in 2025 . Like Stripes, Voice of America received government funding even as it sometimes reported unfavorably on the government. And like journalists at Stripes , Voice of America reporters have died doing their jobs .

But despite the Trump White House’s unrelenting attacks on public, nonprofit and for-profit media outlets , the government funding model is having some success at the state level. The organization Rebuild Local News estimates that states will spend US$74 million supporting local journalism in 2026 via fellowships, media training, tax credits and more.

While the group’s leaders say these initiatives demand constant scrutiny to ensure there’s no creeping government interference or political strings attached to the funds, many supporters of local journalism see promise in this model . Government funding for independent media has long existed in Europe, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere. Some of these outlets are widely trusted by the public .
But that trust doesn’t come easily. It requires political and military leaders to repeatedly reaffirm the ideal of a free and independent press – even when the coverage doesn’t go their way.
Cindy Elmore was a reporter/photographer for The Stars and Stripes from 1996-2000.

articles.title: Compared to driving, flying is extraordinarily safe – but why doesn’t it feel that way?
articles.author:
<name>Mihhail Berezovski, Associate Professor of Mathematical Sciences, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mihhail-berezovski-2748925"/>
paras: A commercial airplane crash can change how people behave long after the immediate tragedy. News outlets replay the images, people affected share their harrowing stories, and an extraordinarily rare event becomes easy to imagine. Some travelers cancel trips; others drive to their destination instead .
These choices may feel cautious. Statistically, the alternatives people switch to may come with greater risk.

Commercial airline crashes command attention because they are rare, catastrophic and beyond a passenger’s control. But the choice to avoid flying does not eliminate risk. As a new report from our research team at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University outlines , skipping a flight and opting to drive instead is typically much riskier, even if it doesn’t feel like it.

People tend to respond strongly to events that are vivid, while paying less attention to familiar hazards – the risks of which manifest more frequently but less visibly. As a result, efforts to avoid one danger can create another.

In our recent peer-reviewed report , prepared with support from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Boeing Center for Aviation and Aerospace Safety, we compared fatality risk in U.S. commercial aviation with other transportation modes, recreational activities, household hazards and occupational risks. While the Boeing Center receives some funding from The Boeing Company, it operates independently.

We focused on commercial Part 121 airlines operating in the U.S. and analyzed data from 2016 through 2025. Part 121 carriers generally include large U.S. airlines and regional carriers that operate scheduled passenger service. Because fatal accidents are so rare, data from a single year would not have provided a stable risk estimate.

Across several measures of risk exposure, including distance traveled, individual boardings, hours spent traveling, annual risk and lifetime odds, the data consistently shows that U.S. commercial aviation is exceptionally safe.

For the same distance traveled, we estimated the fatality risk as about 626 times higher in a passenger car or truck than on a commercial airline. The risk associated with motorcycle travel was more than 22,000 times higher than commercial airline travel. Even highway bus travel, itself a relatively safe option, carried about nine times the risk of commercial airline travel over the same distance.

When risk is measured per passenger boarding, the numbers remain striking. From 2016 through 2024, the long-run estimate was approximately one passenger fatality per 97.7 million boardings on commercial airlines.

These numbers do not mean flying is risk-free, just that the risk is small enough that researchers need many years and enormous amounts of exposure to estimate it. Across the 10-year study period, 73 people died in accidents involving commercial airline travel in the United States.

These findings complement earlier research. A peer-reviewed 2013 study comparing U.S. transportation modes examined data from 2000 through 2009 and also identified commercial aviation as the safest way to travel. A 2018 study using data from the same period similarly ranked commercial aviation as the safest mode.

More recently, a 2022 study analyzed U.S. news coverage, travel patterns and accident data from 1996 through 2017. It found that increased news coverage of aviation accidents was associated with more road traffic and more fatal road accidents in subsequent months.

The aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks provided a powerful example of how behavior can shift risk from one setting to another. Air travel declined sharply after the 9/11 attacks. Subsequently, researchers were able to investigate whether fear of flying led to additional deaths on the road.

Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer analyzed traffic patterns for the final three months of 2001 and estimated 353 excess road deaths nationwide. He characterized many people’s decision to drive rather than fly as an attempt to avoid a “dread risk”: a low-probability event in which many people could die at once.

Transportation researchers Michael Sivak and Michael Flannagan later reanalyzed the period . They used road fatality trends from the first eight months of 2000 and 2001 to estimate how many deaths would normally have occurred during the final three months of 2001. They then compared that estimate with the number actually recorded in the past three months and calculated 1,018 additional road fatalities from October 2001 through December 2001.

But their findings complicated the idea that people who avoided flying merely drove to the same distant destinations. Much of the increase occurred on local roads , not interstate highways, and pedestrians and bicyclists experienced a disproportionate share of fatalities. This pattern suggests that travel behavior may have changed more broadly after the attacks, perhaps because people canceled longer trips, stayed closer to home or changed their daily routines.

It is hard to pin down how much of this increase was related to people changing their travel patterns in response to the 9/11 attacks, since these studies cannot track each individual’s transportation decisions.

But both studies suggest that a collective effort to avoid a highly visible danger can increase exposure to ordinary hazards whose victims are less visible. When more people choose to drive rather than fly, the roads become busier and the number of traffic deaths can rise.
One reason discussions about risk become confusing is that there is no single way to measure it. The answer to the question “Is it safe?” depends on what you measure.

How much risk does a person face for each mile traveled? What is the risk of one trip? How much risk accumulates during one hour of travel? What is the chance of dying from this cause in a year or over a lifetime?

These are legitimate questions, but to make a valid comparison, you need to look at the same measure of risk for both types of transportation. Comparing the risk of one flight with the annual risk of driving, for example, mixes unlike quantities.

A traveler deciding whether to fly or drive between two cities can compare the two modes over the same trip or distance. This comparison provides a clearer perspective than comparing a highly visible plane crash with a familiar daily routine.
Time matters too. In our estimates, an hour in a passenger car or truck carried about 74 times the fatality risk of an hour aboard a commercial aircraft.

Driving gives people a steering wheel, a brake pedal and the belief that their skill can protect them. Flying asks passengers to place control in the hands of pilots, airlines, regulators, air traffic controllers and a complex technical system. Psychological research has linked a stronger sense of agency – the feeling that people control their actions and their outcomes – with greater risk-taking. That difference in perceived control helps explain why a rare aviation disaster can feel more threatening than routine road travel.

Media attention also matters. A major airplane crash is treated as news of national or international importance. Road deaths occur across many locations and at different times, so the public does not see the cumulative toll.
The emotional intensity of coverage does not mean journalists are wrong to cover crashes. It just means audiences need context alongside the images.

Telling anxious travelers that flying is “safe” is rarely enough. Research on risk perception shows that people do not judge danger through statistics alone. Fear and vivid images also shape how risky an event feels. But providing more context about the risks from other forms of transportation can still help.

Effective communication about risk does not minimize tragedy or dismiss the real fear people may feel. But it can help people understand that when millions of travelers shift from one type of transportation to another, the risk moves with them.

For travelers, the practical question is not whether an option has zero risk. No option does. The question is whether a choice reduces their total exposure to risk or merely replaces a frightening, highly visible risk with a greater one that feels routine.

To put the rarity of fatal airline events into perspective, an average of 2.48 million travelers passed through TSA screening each day in 2025. Modern commercial aviation in the United States has achieved a safety record that is difficult to grasp precisely because fatal events are so unusual.
When fear leads people away from that system, the safest-feeling decision may not be the safest decision at all.

articles.title: In Colorado and elsewhere, sexual assault peaks on campuses at the beginning of the school year – here’s what students should know
articles.author:
<name>Kaitlyn M. Sims, Assistant Professor of Public Policy, University of Denver; Institute for Humane Studies</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kaitlyn-m-sims-2272597"/>
paras: With the start of the new fall semester, students are gearing up for football season, homecoming celebrations and a new round of academic coursework. Yet the first weeks of the fall term are also a time for caution.

The so-called red zone is the period when college students’ risk of being sexually assaulted is highest. According to a 2019 campus climate survey – one of the most recent studies of its size – first-year women are at the highest risk.

In a survey of nine U.S. colleges, over half of campus sexual assaults of first-year students occurred between orientation and Halloween. Data collected by the University of Colorado at Boulder’s Office of Institutional Equity and Compliance in 2021 and 2024 show that the majority of assaults of first-year women students took place in September or October.

Statewide data on self-reported campus sexual assault isn’t collected, but cases associated with several major universities in Colorado in 2026 highlight the issue. In March 2026, Boulder police investigated a series of sexual assaults of underage women at a popular University Hill bar. The women were allegedly drugged, and the bar lost its liquor license and closed permanently.
In July 2026, parents of an Air Force Academy graduate who died by suicide filed a federal lawsuit alleging the university failed to protect their daughter from sexual assault.

As a researcher who studies domestic and interpersonal violence – and a college professor who works with students every day – I’m well aware that estimates of student sexual assault often understate the problem. Students often do not report an assault because they don’t know where to turn, have concerns about confidentiality, don’t trust the institution to respond adequately or are unable to navigate the institution’s resources by themselves. This parallels vast underreporting of sexual assault and abuse in general.
But the number of cases that are reported is already cause for concern.

While campus sexual assault is a well-known issue, data on the current state of the problem is limited. Under the Clery Act, federally funded colleges must report annual crime and safety data , but these include sexual assaults only if they are formally reported. If only 16% of victims report their assault through formal channels, this dramatically undercounts students’ experiences of campus sexual assault.

As of 2022, federal law requires universities to conduct campus climate surveys every two years using a standardized tool created by the Department of Education . However, the department has not yet published the survey or the web portal that Congress has charged it with creating.

The best data we do have comes from private groups. The Association of American Universities ran campus climate surveys in 2015 and 2019 . WeStat ran a 2024 survey of 10 largely private, largely East Coast universities. But infrequent surveys from private companies are subject to their own discretion and timing, making them less reliable than regular data collected by public agencies.
Surveys consistently estimate 1 in 5 college women are assaulted while attending university . Students from marginalized groups, including gender or sexual minorities, are at higher risk .
Risks are also higher for students involved in fraternities or sororities .

First-year women are at the highest risk . These students are particularly vulnerable because they are in a new environment, have fewer friends to watch their back and are often exploring new freedoms, including access to alcohol and other drugs. In addition, many students attend college away from their hometowns where they are separated from their support networks.
Counter to the popular perception that perpetrators are unknown assailants, most sexual assaults are perpetrated by someone known to the victim , and over 21% are committed by an intimate partner.

Alcohol and other drug use creates an especially high risk for sexual assault. While young adults ages 18-25 are drinking less than prior generations , a quarter of surveyed full-time college students reported binge drinking in the previous month . Campus climate surveys show that a majority of surveyed students who were assaulted had voluntarily consumed alcohol and other drugs prior to the assault.
To be clear, these studies are not blaming anyone who has been victimized for drinking. Rather, the research points out how alcohol and other drugs can increase a person’s vulnerability.
College sexual assault substantially affects students’ well-being.

Students who are sexually assaulted are at higher risk for reporting anxiety and depression . Adverse mental and physical health effects of college sexual assault can last for years after graduation .
Sexual assault also negatively affects education outcomes. Students who are assaulted are more likely to have lower grades and learning difficulties – or drop out of college altogether.

Schools receiving federal funding have a legal obligation under Title IX to respond to allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment. This 1972 federal law prohibits sex-based discrimination in education programs , including on college campuses.

But for students who are victimized during the red zone, accessing care on campus may be particularly challenging. New students, such as freshmen and transfer students, may be less familiar with available resources and their legal rights .
Schools have tried a number of strategies to address the red zone and keep students safe.

Web-based interventions and small-group intensives can reduce victimization, improve students’ self-defense measures, reduce binge drinking and improve bystander intervention awareness . Bystander intervention training teaches students to safely step in when they see unsafe behavior.

These programs help students change their behaviors – such as reducing binge drinking – and combat pervasive “rape myths,” or the belief that victims of sexual assault were “asking for it.” Positive effects can continue years after students complete the training program .
Truly tackling the issue of college sexual assault requires developing new ways to stop individuals who may go on to assault others.

But the focus remains on teaching potential victims how to defend themselves and look out for their peers. Researchers know much, much less about interventions that can prevent people from perpetrating sexual assaults.

In part, this research gap exists because it is difficult to get accurate data on socially undesirable behaviors . Research has shown that survey and interview respondents may misreport their beliefs or behaviors , meaning that people who commit assault are unlikely to admit that on a survey. Certain research methods, such as using written or web-based surveys rather than face-to-face interviews, can elicit more truthful responses.

In Colorado and at colleges across the country, now is the time to keep an eye out for the most vulnerable students. Faculty, staff, students and community members alike can all help build a campus climate where sexual assault is unacceptable, where victims are believed, and where student safety matters.
If you or someone you know has been affected by sexual assault, help is available. RAINN operates a 24/7 helpline at 800-656-HOPE.
Kaitlyn M. Sims is an Assistant Professor at the University of Denver and a criminal justice research fellow at Arnold Ventures.

articles.title: AI skin cancer detection tools are getting better – but only for people with light skin
articles.author:
<name>Mohamed Akrout, Assistant Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Tennessee</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mohamed-akrout-2605973"/>
paras: Imagine you’re getting out of the shower one morning and you notice a mole on your thigh that you’ve never seen before. It’s reddish brown, bumpy and surprisingly large. Is it a benign mole, or is it melanoma ?

A slew of new artificial intelligence tools claim they can help you figure it out . Some are smartphone apps that anyone can download to scan their skin at home, while others are software programs designed to be used directly by clinicians in a doctor’s office.

As a computer engineer studying how tools like these perform in real-world clinical settings , I know that finding a way to accurately use AI in dermatology would be immensely valuable to patients around the world. It could offer broad access to medical expertise, providing lifesaving screenings to remote areas or underresourced communities where dermatologists are scarce.

But at the moment, these tools have a crucial shortcoming that researchers will have to resolve: They are increasingly accurate for people with light skin – but they have a massive blind spot when it comes to analyzing darker skin.
The central myth of AI is that it functions objectively . In reality, an AI model is simply a pattern-matching engine. It learns to associate certain visual features with certain diseases.

But it can easily be thrown off by the background color of a person’s skin. In other words, the AI model doesn’t learn to look at the lesion itself. Instead, it picks up on the color of the surrounding skin as a clue. This means that the model’s ability to make accurate predictions essentially degrades to guesses based on skin color.

My colleagues and I found that the ability of these tools to accurately diagnose skin conditions dropped significantly when we simply darkened the surrounding skin on patients’ images. We trained an AI model on photographs of known skin conditions in light-skinned patients, then digitally manipulated the images to resemble darker skin tones. The clinical condition in the photo had not changed, but the AI’s ability to recognize it deteriorated sharply.

For example, consider a condition such as atopic dermatitis – a chronic, itchy and inflammatory skin disease. It causes a skin discoloration that appears pink on light skin but gray or violet on darker skin. Our research and that of other groups shows that AI models would reliably classify the pink marks but might not identify the darker colors as signs of atopic dermatitis.

This AI classification blind spot means that patients with darker skin would receive measurably worse care . The disparity has critical consequences because skin cancers such as melanoma are visually harder to spot on pigmented skin. Patients of color are already more likely to be diagnosed at a more advanced stage , which leads to significantly lower survival rates. A diagnostic tool that works better for people with lighter skin only widens this gap.

This bias extends beyond tools used by clinicians to more widely used AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT or Claude. The stakes can become higher when people turn to these tools for medical answers without a clinician to double-check the output, making accuracy across all skin tones a matter of patient safety.

In a 2024 study, we presented OpenAI’s model, GPT-4, with an image of a completely benign mole. When we digitally darkened the skin around the mole while keeping the mole itself exactly the same, GPT-4 classified the spot as malignant melanoma. Because the skin color is the more prominent feature, the AI became so focused on the dark pigment of the skin that it ignored the standard medical rules used to identify cancer, such as checking whether the mole’s borders are irregular.
If a person uses these tools at home, a harmless dark spot might trigger unnecessary panic, while a life-threatening cancer on dark skin could be overlooked.
Why does this bias exist? The answer lies in the images used to train AI models.
Researchers build these AI models by feeding them hundreds of thousands of images pulled from public online libraries of medical photos shared by universities and hospitals.

Historically, these medical databases – as well as dermatology textbooks – have been dominated by images of lighter skin tones . Darker skin images are relatively rare, in part because clinical norms were developed primarily around white patients. If an AI model is never taught what melanoma looks like on dark skin, it simply won’t know how to find it.

To achieve the same accuracy on darker skin as on lighter skin, these models need a more diverse set of images for training. However, while there are millions of photos of light-skinned patients already available in historical databases, gathering a massive new database of real photos from patients of color raises challenging ethical and patient privacy issues.

One way around this privacy hurdle may be to use generative AI – the same technology powering chatbots, which can also be used to make deepfake videos – to artificially generate thousands of synthetic medical images.

Using just text prompts, researchers can create realistic, high-quality images of conditions such as melanoma on darker skin tones. My colleagues and I showed that an AI trained entirely on these synthetic images can learn to correctly categorize data using those images just as well as one trained on real ones.

However, this approach carries a hidden risk: Generative AI models can create high-quality images, but they may not map cleanly onto the characteristics of skin conditions that patients actually experience. This would be like using an inaccurate map to teach someone how to navigate.

If researchers train a diagnostic AI tool on these flawed synthetic images, the data might look perfectly diverse on a spreadsheet, but the tool will remain functionally blind to how these diseases actually appear on real patients of color.

At the moment, there is no shortcut around this problem. The only viable path forward is to build more inclusive and representative collections of images, particularly from people with darker skin tones.

Today, the medical AI field is at a crossroads. While some of these AI skin-scanning tools are already making their way into clinics and app stores for use in the U.S. and around the world, researchers and regulators are already pushing for stricter testing across all skin tones before these tools are widely deployed.
Ultimately, eliminating color-based bias in AI isn’t just about fairness, but rather the absolute baseline required to ensure these tools actually work for the people who need them most.

Mohamed Akrout does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: BNSF Demands Cloud Seattle's Path to Replacing Aging Jackson Street Bridges
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Aging segments of Seattle's downtown street grid around King Street Station would not be able to be rebuilt at their existing heights if they needed to be replaced, according to a newly released study from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). A bridge over BNSF railroad tracks that carries South Jackson Street and Second Avenue Extension S would need to be three to seven feet higher to receive railroad buy in, a fact that would have cascading effects on access to other nearby streets and properties.

SDOT's study was part of its Bridge Replacement and Rehabilitation Program. It looked at the early 1900s-era S Jackson Street bridge between Third and Fourth Avenue – known as Bridge 7 – and another smaller bridge to the east in front of Union Station, known as Bridge 33W. Both bridges were rehabilitated in the 1980s, and seismically retrofitted to withstand earthquakes more recently.

Nonetheless, City engineers have determined both bridges have surpassed their design life and could ultimately need to be replaced. This is a significant challenge given the fact that they provide critical connections for people across Seattle and the entire region, with more than 1,400 buses traversing them every weekday.

"With regular maintenance and monitoring, many bridges last well beyond their design life but it is still important to plan ahead especially when the need for future rehabilitation and replacement is not driven by a poor bridge condition state," the study's executive summary states.

Any replacement bridge over the railroad tracks would need to be significantly higher than today's conditions because the existing bridge doesn't meet current requirements for vertical clearance above BNSF's right-of-way. Such a change would have major impacts on nearby properties, including an entrance to Sound Transit's Sounder commuter rail platform, and the King Street Station entrance plaza. Near bridge 33W, the Icon Apartments sit directly along the sidewalk, with a potential seven foot increase in height something that would block most of the ground floor.

"Improving the vertical clearance to meeting BNSF’s requirements would result in a grade rise of S Jackson Street between 3 and 7 feet, depending on the replacement concept," the summary states. "This change in grade would require 4th Avenue S to also be replaced and would affect access to properties adjacent to 4th Avenue S, S Jackson Street, and potentially along 2nd Avenue Extension S."

The cost of a replacement for Bridge 7 was pegged at anywhere from $99 million to $210 million, but any required height increase would also necessitate replacing Bridge 33W, at a cost of another $32 to $66 million. The study did look at what a retrofit for Bridge 7 would look like, but found that option would cost up to $160 million and take up to 12 years, due to a narrow window of construction work that BNSF would allow within its right-of-way – crews could only work four hours every day.

What it would look like to rebuild the Fourth Avenue S Viaduct was not addressed in the study, but those costs are likely to dwarf the costs of the smaller two bridges it sits between. In 2020, SDOT released the news that costs to seismically retrofit the Fourth Avenue bridge, from S Main Street south to Seattle Boulevard, had to be revised upward by a factor of more than 12, from $8.6 million to $109.4 million.

This cluster of interconnected bridges in south downtown has been in the crosshairs for a number of years, as Sound Transit has continued to advance alternatives for a second light rail tunnel through downtown as part of the Ballard Link Extension. It was partly the narrow construction window set by BNSF, on top of other potential technical hurdles, that have pushed Sound Transit away from considering a route under Fourth Avenue, with a third-party consultant calling the option "not reasonably constructible."

The need to retrofit these bridges has also been an issue in the context of the Center City Connector, with a 2024 study concluding that upgrades would be needed to handle the new, heavier streetcar vehicles that would be a component of bridging the city's existing streetcar lines together via First Avenue.
But even if Sound Transit passes the area by and the streetcar remains on ice, these bridges aren't getting any younger.

The $1.55 billion transportation levy that voters approved in 2024 included $221 million for bridges, but most of that funding was earmarked for bridge repair and maintenance, not any full bridge replacements. The levy set aside $20 million to be divvied up among six bridge projects in the hopes of seeking future construction funding, but higher priority bridges like the Magnolia Bridge, and the First and Fourth Avenue bridges further south in SoDo over the Argo railyard, made the cut ahead of Bridge 7 or 33W.

The City could save money on a replacement for Bridge 7 by building an arch bridge over the BNSF right-of-way, just four feet over the existing bridge – but that option was all but rejected due to its impact on traffic. The arch bridge concept would have been expected to cost between $68 million and $145 million, or $65 million less than the high-end cost for the full replacement.

"One concept included removal of the portion of the Bridge 7 structure under 2nd Avenue Extension S, south of S Jackson Street," the study summary noted. "However, preliminary traffic analysis showed that these changes to roadway network and circulation in the neighborhood would not be feasible with today’s bus and vehicle volumes."
The bridge planning study's executive summary stops short of making a recommendation, but SDOT's project website does go a step further in summarizing where things currently stand.

"While we have not selected a preferred alternative, bridge replacement is looking like it would be a better investment in the long-term," the newly updated webpage notes. "Any of the options will be expensive, require railroad coordination, take time to construct, and cause disruption to the surrounding neighborhoods. We will need to be creative and opportunistic in our approach to funding and delivering this project."

The state of these bridges is unlikely to become a live issue in the immediate future, but this study does put some major issues on the table that future generations of Seattle leaders are likely going to grapple with – and that could leave Jackson Street looking very different than it does today.

articles.title: Why Seattle waste drivers aren’t getting pricked like sanitation workers in New York (but you should still dispose of your needles in a safer way)
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Automated garbage can lifts mostly protect Seattle collection drivers as the city’s garbage and recycling systems deal with an increase in consumer hypodermic needle use.

Seattle Public Utilities tells CHS it has not recorded an increase in needlestick injuries among contractors servicing the city. Unlike cities where crews manually lift trash bags, Seattle’s residential routes use mechanical arms to empty curbside carts directly into trucks, keeping drivers away from thin bags and protruding needles.

Cities with manual collection face different hazards. In New York City, where Department of Sanitation crews lift bags by hand, the agency has logged 49 needlestick injuries through early August. That surpassed the 46 incidents reported in 2025 and rose from 18 in 2020. The increase led New York to raise fines for improper needle disposal from $100 to $250. DSNY does not test recovered needles, but officials attribute the rise to more residents using at-home injectable drugs.

Manual collection remains standard in older, denser East Coast cities where narrow streets and row homes prevent automated side-loader trucks from operating. In Philadelphia, the city’s Community Life Improvement Program and Department of Sanitation deploy specialized teams equipped with puncture-resistant gear to clear corridors like Kensington, where union representatives with AFSCME District Council 33 have cited worker safety and punctures from loose needles during manual trash collection. In Boston, where contracted haulers physically toss bags into rear compactors, city public health officials conduct targeted daily needle sweeps along high-traffic corridors like the “Mass and Cass” area to clear loose syringes before curbside collection begins.

The municipal strain follows a broader shift documented by The New York Times , which reported last month that syringes and auto-injectors have migrated from clinical settings directly onto domestic bathroom vanities. According to the report, nearly one in five U.S. adults has tried an injectable GLP-1 medication like Ozempic, while consumer interest in injectable peptides and at-home fertility treatments like IVF — which grew nearly 40% between 2018 and 2026 — has routinely pushed medical sharps into households.

That proliferation has created new hazards in our waste The New York Times reports sanitation workers there frequently encounter exposed, loose needles when lifting plastic garbage bags, with one New York City department supervisor telling the paper that crews regularly open bags to find needles completely unshielded. The surge is also hitting retail businesses. The Times cited a Nordstrom Rack restroom that posted signs pleading with shoppers to stop dropping GLP-1 syringes into its public sharps containers due to the escalating fees the retailer pays to empty them.

SPU says that it does not track the source or type of discarded needles, meaning it cannot link box totals to specific drugs like GLP-1 weight-loss medications. While automated trucks protect Seattle drivers, the machinery does not protect downstream workers.

Washington law and King County health rules prohibit sharps in household garbage or curbside recycling. SPU directs residents to use puncture-resistant containers and drop them at public boxes or the North Transfer Station.

Improperly discarded sharps still reach sorting plants. Industry publications note that because retail pharmacies rarely provide mail-back boxes with injectable prescriptions, people often throw pens into the trash or stash needles in milk jugs and soda bottles sent to recycling.

Compactors inside automated trucks crush those plastic jugs, scattering loose needles into the sorting stream. According to the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, needlestick wounds risk exposure to hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

The danger then falls on sorting facilities, where workers manually pull recyclables off conveyor belts. A study by the Environmental Research & Education Foundation and the Solid Waste Association of North America estimated somewhere around 1,000 needlestick injuries happen annually at recycling facilities, with manual sorters injured at a rate of 3.9 per 100 workers. More than half of surveyed facilities report finding loose needles mixed into recyclables daily or weekly.

A few drugmakers and select specialty pharmacies provide free mail-back sharps containers for specific injectables, but standard retail pharmacies rarely include disposal with prescriptions. As a result, safe disposal largely depends on state initiatives — such as Washington’s free prepaid injector mail-back service — and municipal drop-off sites provided by utilities like SPU.

Seattle’s tough years of drug crisis including spikes in intravenous drug use may be helping keep workers safe from the pricks. Seattle Public Utilities maintains 23 public drop boxes across the city for safe disposal. The disposal boxes, located on city property and public rights-of-way such as exterior restroom walls in parks like Cal Anderson , are heavy-duty, tamper-resistant deposit chutes. Residents drop sealed containers into the chute directly at any time.

Seattle’s drop boxes are also busier. SPU reports it collected 446,716 sharps through its 23 public drop boxes through the first half of 2026 — about 22% more than the pace in the previous two years. It’s unknown how many of the rest of those needles are taking a dangerous path to the landfill or recycling plant.
Learn more from King County Public Health on how to safely dispose of needles at home .

articles.title: At Sea’d In, the wood fire is burning again in Capitol Hill’s Chophouse Row
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Two of the most important names in the Pike/Pine business community are behind the creation of Sea’d In , a new Capitol Hill restaurant that treats fish like fine steak.

Chef Heong Soon Park said the spark for the wood fire-powered concept came in a call from Chophouse Row developer Liz Dunn , who Park credits with keeping Capitol Hill’s character intact as the neighborhood changes and grows. She had a showcase restaurant space open and one question for him up front: Did he like cooking with fire?

Park had already been circling an idea for a seafood restaurant, something he had originally pictured closer to the water, but that concept never found the right home. When Dunn reached out, he brought the idea to her instead, and the two of them worked out the shape of it together. “She inspired me, and then I filled in the blanks,” he says.

While Dunn — Chophouse Row, the Piston & Ring Building, Melrose Market — is the shaper of many of the core commercial spaces of modern-day Capitol Hill, Park is responsible for a growing fleet of neighborhood restaurants.

Park’s first venture in Capitol Hill’s restaurant scene was Meet Korean BBQ which has been part of Capitol Hill since its inauspicious opening in the winter of 2020 only weeks before the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns hit.

In 2024, Park took on the reinvention of a space that had been home to a deeply rooted Capitol Hill food legend with the transformation that saw his Grana Padano and Parmesan-laden Cheese Room take over the longtime Melrose at Pine home of Machiavelli as its ownership decided to focus on its Edmonds location.
Park’s most recent Capitol Hill reboot came last year on E Pike where he opened Gol Mok Korean Market Bar , a new start for the Taku space created by Seattle celebrity chef Shota Nakajima .
Other recent acquisitions include restarts in West Seattle including the Luna Park Cafe .
Park’s new beginnings aren’t shallow imitations. He has been part of the Seattle dining scene for 20 years and owns Chan in the Paramount Hotel downtown and the Bacco Café in Pike Place Market .

Sea’d In is also much more than a reboot. The restaurant’s identity is in dry-aged seafood and techniques Park traces back to South Korea where cooks didn’t have the cold storage geography of Europe and instead learned to age fish in the cold sea air.

Seafood comes in from auction and gets handled as little as possible before going into an aging room held between roughly 0 and 5 degrees Celsius, with humidity between 70 and 90%. Timing depends on the fish. White fish like snapper or branzino ages three to four days, salmon two to three weeks, and tuna, because of its higher fat content, as long as two months. It’s the same protein and enzyme breakdown that tenderizes dry aged beef, drawing out moisture and concentrating flavor.
From there, everything goes onto Sea’d In’s wood fired grill, the only cooking method in the space formerly home to the Light Sleeper wine bar and once home to long-gone Bar Ferdinand .

“We start with this basic fish, we layer it with the dry age, we layer it with the smoke, we layer with koji, we layer with the sauce,” Park says. That idea of stacking time and technique is where the restaurant’s “Time and Fire” comes from. Time is aging and fermenting. Then comes the fire.

Park says this project might be his favorite of anything he’s done, largely because of the Chophouse Row and its courtyard. There is live music on weekends, a monthly art night, and an annual local fashion show, plus neighbors like Xóm and Tailwind Cafe .
“This is exactly how Capitol Hill used to be. Nothing crazy, always chill, happy, relaxed,” he says. “Now I feel like I’m part of it.”
For a first visit, he recommends the crudo, all of it dry-aged, along with vegetables cooked over the wood fire and a whole fish that’s gone through the full aging and grilling process.
“Come in here or sit in the courtyard and enjoy the weather. You don’t have to be on your phone anymore,” Park says. “This is a good place to know neighbors. Meet actual people here.”
Sea’d In now open inside Chophouse Row at 1124 11th Ave. Learn more at seadinseattle.com .

articles.title: Seattle students head to class as district and teachers union reach agreement
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Seattle Public Schools and the Seattle Education Association reached a tentative contract agreement late Tuesday clearing the way for classes to begin on schedule Wednesday morning.

The deal averts a strike across the district which serves some 50,000 students and employs 6,000 union-represented educators and staff . Students in grades 1 through 12 return to classrooms on September 2, followed by preschool and kindergarten students on September 8 . The contract remains subject to ratification votes by both the union membership and the Seattle School Board .

Specifics of the tentative deal including final salary schedules were not disclosed in the joint announcement but the union said the sides reached “agreements” on all 52 issues raised in the negotiations.

The tentative agreement reportedly is centered on the district’s officer of an 8.8% baseline salary increase over three years, broken down into annual bumps of 2.6%, 3.6%, and 2.6%. This raise passes through projected state-funded cost-of-living adjustments with no furlough days, alongside standard annual experience step increases averaging roughly 4% for eligible staff.

CHS reported here on what was at stake as the district’s contract package would pass through projected state-funded cost-of-living adjustments with no local increase. The Seattle Education Association was proposing the same state inflation adjustment plus an additional 6.0% wage increase over three years, alongside targeted bumps for paraprofessionals and office staff.

Additional provisions including new psychologists, assigning a full-time social worker or counselor to schools with more than 350 students, and restructuring special education models to keep students in neighborhood schools with increased behavioral support were also on the table.
The district proposal also featured SPS-funded health accounts, reduced monthly staff meetings, and an additional paid training day for more than 1,500 paraprofessionals and office staff.

The negotiations follow the union’s previous three-year collective bargaining agreement reached in September 2022. That deal provided a 7% raise in year one, 4% in year two, and 3% in year three, alongside cost-of-living adjustments tied to the state Implicit Price Deflator. That established a 14% baseline wage increase over the life of the contract.
The median and average salary for Seattle Public Schools teachers sits at approximately $117,000 per year.

Seattle’s public school district is facing ongoing challenges amid falling enrollment. Enrollment is hovering around 49,000 students, representing a drop of roughly 4,500 to 5,000 students from its pre-pandemic peak of 53,627 in 2019–2020. Elementary buildings are currently operating at an average of roughly 65% capacity, well below the district’s 85% target. The primary driver of the long-term decline is smaller incoming classes.

The district’s plan to shutter under-enrolled elementary schools including Stevens Elementary on Capitol Hill was met with strong public backlash in 2024 but the economic factors driving the push have not improved.

The district is facing ongoing structural budget deficits, operating with an annual general fund budget of roughly $1.35 billion while managing annual shortfalls in the $90 million to $130 million range. The state allocates school funding primarily on a per-pupil model. With its enrollment dropping, SPS loses tens of millions annually in state basic education funding. Meanwhile, federal pandemic relief funds have fully expired.
Superintendent Ben Shuldiner praised the bargaining teams and SEA leadership for reaching an agreement that keeps classrooms safe and supportive while allowing schools to open on time.
“Educators are fierce advocates for our students and SEA members made this agreement possible through strength and unity,” SEA vice president and lead bargainer Davina Diaz said.
